sections.body_md:
Affine scaling stays in the interior of a standard-form linear program and follows a scaled steepest-descent direction. The objective is linear, so an unscaled steepest step is just a multiple of the cost, and it will usually leave the affine set \(A x = b\). The scaling and a projection put it back.

At a strictly positive \(x\), let \(X\) be the diagonal matrix of those coordinates. The local model minimizes the linear cost plus a squared length \(d^T X^{-2} d\), subject to \(A d = 0\). The squared length is large where a coordinate is small, so the step is reluctant to approach the wall. The minimizer is \(d = -X^2 (c - A^T y)\), where the dual estimate \(y\) solves the scaled normal equation \(A X^2 A^T y = A X^2 c\). That choice is exactly what makes \(A d = 0\).

The direction usually has some negative components. Each of those components reaches zero at the step length \(x_i / |d_i|\). The iteration takes a fraction of the smallest such length, with the fraction strictly below one, so the next point stays positive and the next diagonal is defined. A full step to the wall would zero a coordinate and stop the formula.

The same construction on the dual slacks is dual affine scaling. Neither version is a simplex pivot, which walks an edge and lands on a vertex. Affine scaling cuts through the interior.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
With \(X = \mathrm{diag}(x)\) and \(x > 0\),
\[
A X^2 A^T y = A X^2 c, \qquad d = -X^2 (c - A^T y).
\]
The step is \(x + \alpha d\) with \(\alpha = \gamma \min_{d_i < 0} (-x_i / d_i)\) and \(\gamma \in (0,\ 1)\). The model being minimized in \(d\) is \(c^T d + \tfrac12 d^T X^{-2} d\) subject to \(A d = 0\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Minimize \(x_1 + 2 x_2\) subject to \(x_1 + x_2 = 6\), starting at \((3,\ 3)\). The squared diagonal entries are \(9\) and \(9\). The normal coefficient is \(18\), and the right-hand side is \(9 \cdot 1 + 9 \cdot 2 = 27\). The dual estimate is \(27/18 = 3/2\). The reduced costs are \((1 - 3/2,\ 2 - 3/2) = (-1/2,\ 1/2)\). The direction is \(-9\) times that vector, which is \((9/2,\ -9/2)\).

The ferry coordinate is 4.5. The second component is negative, so the blocking step is \(3 / (9/2) = 2/3\). Half of that step has length \(1/3\). The new point is \((3,\ 3) + (1/3)(9/2,\ -9/2) = (4.5,\ 1.5)\). It stays on the line \(x_1 + x_2 = 6\), and both coordinates stay positive. Subtracting the direction would have moved toward the more expensive vertex.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The direction is added. Subtracting it follows the reduced costs uphill. A second slip is to take the fraction equal to one and then form a new diagonal. A zero coordinate makes \(X^{-2}\) undefined. A third is to forget the dual estimate and step along \(-c\). That vector need not satisfy \(A d = 0\), so the next point leaves the affine set. A fourth is to treat the method as a simplex pivot. No basis is chosen, and the point does not sit at a vertex. Scaling by \(X\) instead of \(X^2\) is a fifth slip. The metric is \(X^{-2}\), so the normal equation uses the square.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Putting a positive target back into the complementarity products, and linearizing the whole perturbed system by Newton, is a primal-dual interior-point step. Affine scaling corresponds to the pure predictor direction in which that target is zero and only the primal scaling is visible. The interior-point step keeps a positive target, moves the slacks as well as \(x\), and shortens the Newton step so both stay positive.
